### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture

**Concise Recognizable Title:** *Guevara v. Inocentes*

**Full Official Caption:** Onofre P. Guevara, Petitioner, vs. Raoul M. Inocentes, Respondent.

**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. L-25577; March 15, 1966; 123 Phil. 200; En Banc; Ponente: Bautista Angelo, J.
- Voting Breakdown: 
  - Concurring: Bengzon, C.J., Reyes, J.B.L., Barrera, Regala, Concepcion (separate concurring opinion), and Dizon (separate concurring opinion) JJ.
  - Dissenting: Makalintal, J. (reiterating his dissent from the resolution of February 16, 1966).
  - Took No Part: Bengzon, J.P., and Sanchez, JJ.

**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
- **Onofre P. Guevara (Petitioner):** Recipient of an *ad interim* appointment as Undersecretary of Labor issued on November 18, 1965, by outgoing President Diosdado Macapagal.
- **Raoul M. Inocentes (Respondent):** Recipient of a rival *ad interim* appointment to the identical position of Undersecretary of Labor issued on January 23, 1966, by incoming President Ferdinand E. Marcos.
- **Diosdado Macapagal:** Outgoing President of the Philippines who issued 1,717 post-election *ad interim* appointments in late 1965 after losing the November 1965 presidential election.
- **Ferdinand E. Marcos:** Incoming President of the Philippines who assumed office on December 30, 1965, convened Congress in special session under Proclamation No. 2, issued Memorandum Circular No. 8 declaring prior unconfirmed *ad interim* appointments lapsed, and appointed Inocentes.

**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Original petition for *quo warranto* filed directly before the Supreme Court under Rule 66 of the Rules of Court, seeking a judicial declaration that Petitioner Guevara is the rightful titleholder of the office of Undersecretary of Labor and challenging the validity of Respondent Inocentes’ appointment and Memorandum Circular No. 8.

---

### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger

**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Executive Department → Power of Appointment → *Ad Interim* Appointments & Termination by Adjournment

**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Legislative Department → Sessions and Adjournment → Special vs. Regular Sessions / Bicameral Adjournment Principles

**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision(s):**

*Historical Constitutional Basis Cited in the Decision:*
Article VII, Section 10, Subsection (4), 1935 Philippine Constitution:
> "The President shall have the power to make appointments during the recess of the Congress, but such appointments shall be effective only until **disapproval by the Commission on Appointments** or **until the next adjournment of the Congress**."

*Modern Counterpart Provision:*
Article VII, Section 16, Paragraph 2, 1987 Philippine Constitution:
> "The President shall have the power to make appointments during the recess of the Congress, whether voluntary or compulsory, but such appointments shall be effective only **until disapproval by the Commission on Appointments** or **until the next adjournment of the Congress**."

**Factual Trigger:** Outgoing President Macapagal issued an *ad interim* appointment to Guevara during congressional recess after losing the November 1965 election; incoming President Marcos called a special congressional session during which the Commission on Appointments was never organized; upon the Senate’s adjournment *sine die* at midnight of January 22, 1966, Marcos declared Guevara’s appointment lapsed via Memorandum Circular No. 8 and appointed Inocentes to the same post, triggering Guevara's petition to reclaim the office.

---

### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard

**November 18, 1965:** Following his defeat in the November 1965 national elections, outgoing President Diosdado Macapagal extends an *ad interim* appointment to Petitioner Onofre P. Guevara as Undersecretary of Labor during the recess of the Fifth Congress.

**November 25, 1965:** Guevara takes his oath of office and assumes the duties of Undersecretary of Labor.

**December 30, 1965:** Ferdinand E. Marcos is inaugurated as President of the Philippines, terminating the Macapagal presidential administration.

**Mid-January 1966:** President Marcos issues Proclamation No. 2 (series of 1966), calling Congress to a special session commencing on January 17, 1966, prior to the scheduled opening of the regular session on the fourth Monday of January.

**January 17–22, 1966:** Congress meets in special session. During this period, neither the Senate nor the House of Representatives organizes the constitutional Commission on Appointments.

**January 22, 1966 (10:55 PM):** The House of Representatives votes to suspend its special session until Monday, January 24, 1966, at 10:00 AM (the statutory commencement hour of the regular session).

**January 22–23, 1966 (past midnight / ~2:00 AM):** The Senate formally adopts a resolution and adjourns the special session *sine die*.

**January 23, 1966 (Sunday):** A non-legislative day intervenes. President Marcos issues Memorandum Circular No. 8, declaring that all *ad interim* appointments extended by the former administration had lapsed and terminated upon the adjournment of the special session of Congress at about midnight of January 22, 1966.

**January 23, 1966:** President Marcos extends an *ad interim* appointment for the position of Undersecretary of Labor to Respondent Raoul M. Inocentes.

**January 24, 1966 (10:00 AM):** The Sixth Congress convenes its first regular session.

**Late January 1966:** Guevara initiates an original petition for *quo warranto* before the Supreme Court, seeking ouster of Inocentes and reinstatement to his post.

**February 16, 1966:** The Supreme Court En Banc promulgates a formal resolution holding that Guevara’s *ad interim* appointment lapsed upon the *sine die* adjournment of the special session at midnight of January 22, 1966.

**March 15, 1966:** The Supreme Court renders its extended full decision explaining the ratio decidendi underlying the February 16, 1966 resolution.

---

### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix

#### A. Petitioner's Arguments (Onofre P. Guevara)

**Main Thesis:** Petitioner holds title to the office under a permanent and valid *ad interim* appointment that could only be terminated by affirmative disapproval of the Commission on Appointments or upon the final adjournment of the 1966 *regular* session of Congress.

**Specific Contentions:**
1. Under Article VII, Section 10(4) of the 1935 Constitution, an *ad interim* appointment is permanent in character and effective until either express disapproval by the Commission on Appointments or the adjournment of the regular annual session.
2. The Commission on Appointments was never organized or constituted during the special session called under Proclamation No. 2; hence, no constitutional body existed that could consider, confirm, or disapprove the appointment.
3. The constitutional phrase "until the next adjournment of the Congress" must be read in tandem with "until disapproval by the Commission on Appointments," meaning the adjournment envisioned is exclusively one wherein a Commission on Appointments had been organized and afforded an opportunity to act.
4. There was no constitutional adjournment on January 22, 1966, because:
   - The House merely *suspended* its session at 10:55 PM to resume on January 24, 1966, at 10:00 AM;
   - The Senate's unilateral resolution to adjourn *sine die* could not constitute an adjournment of "the Congress" as a collective bicameral body;
   - The suspension by the House and resumption on Monday morning created a continuous, uninterrupted session blending the special session directly into the regular session.

#### B. Respondent's Arguments (Raoul M. Inocentes & Solicitor General)

**Main Thesis:** Petitioner’s appointment expired automatically as a matter of law upon the adjournment *sine die* of the special session of Congress on January 22, 1966, rendering the office vacant for Respondent’s valid appointment.

**Specific Contentions:**
1. Petitioner's *ad interim* appointment lapsed when Congress adjourned its special session under Proclamation No. 2; the Constitution does not distinguish between regular and special sessions.
2. Under general constitutional tenets, an *ad interim* appointment ceases to be valid after each term of Congress, having lapsed as early as December 30, 1965.
3. Petitioner’s appointment was part of a mass rollout of 1,717 post-election "midnight appointments" by an outgoing President, which violates morals, good customs, and public policy, rendering it null and void *ab initio*.
4. Petitioner’s claim is foreclosed under the equitable principles established in *Aytona v. Castillo* and *Rodriguez, Jr. v. Quirino*.

---

### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues

1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not an *ad interim* appointment extended by the President during a congressional recess lapses automatically upon the adjournment of an immediately succeeding *special session* of Congress, even if the Commission on Appointments was not organized during that session.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the special session of Congress adjourned in constitutional contemplation on January 22, 1966, where the Senate adjourned *sine die* while the House of Representatives purported merely to suspend its proceedings until the opening of the regular session on January 24, 1966.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not Petitioner’s appointment can be sustained considering the equitable doctrines governing mass post-election "midnight appointments" laid down in *Aytona v. Castillo*.

---

### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue

#### Issue 1: Lapsation of *Ad Interim* Appointment Upon Adjournment of a Special Session

**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Petitioner’s *ad interim* appointment lapse upon the *sine die* adjournment of the special session of Congress despite the non-organization of the Commission on Appointments?
**YES.** Under Article VII, Section 10(4) of the Constitution, an *ad interim* appointment terminates automatically upon the next adjournment of Congress, whether that session be regular or special, and irrespective of whether the Commission on Appointments was organized.

**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. *Textual Independence of Constitutional Modes:* Article VII, Section 10(4) provides two distinct, disjunctive modes of terminating recess (*ad interim*) appointments: (a) express disapproval by the Commission on Appointments, or (b) the next adjournment of the Congress. These two modes are completely separate and independent. The text does not make the operation of the second mode dependent upon the prior fulfillment of the first.
2. *Avoidance of Absurdity and Obstructionism:* If termination by legislative adjournment were tied to the organization and affirmative action of the Commission on Appointments, a political faction or obstructionist minority controlling Congress could intentionally refuse to organize the Commission. This would confer permanent tenure upon recess appointees without them ever undergoing legislative scrutiny—a result entirely contrary to the constitutional design of checks and balances.
3. *Application of "Ubi Lex Non Distinguit":* The constitutional text refers broadly to "the next adjournment of the Congress" without qualifying whether the session is regular or special. Applying the fundamental statutory maxim *ubi lex non distinguit nec nos distinguere debemus* (where the law does not distinguish, we should not distinguish), the term "adjournment" embraces the termination of either a regular or a special session.
4. *Implied Exercise of Legislative Check:* While appointment is inherently executive, the power to confirm or reject is a legislative check exercised via the Commission on Appointments. If Congress convenes in regular or special session and adjourns without organizing the Commission or acting on recess appointments, it exercises an implied legislative check by permitting the appointments to lapse by constitutional operation.

**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
> "A perusal of the above-quoted provision would at once reveal that it is the clear intent of the framers of our Constitution to make a recess appointment effective only (a) until disapproval by the Commission on Appointments, or (b) until the next adjournment of Congress, and never a day longer regardless of the nature of the session adjourned. ... Hence, the above provision contemplates two modes of termination of an *ad interim* appointment, or of one made during the recess of Congress, which are completely separate from, and independent of, each other."

**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An *ad interim* appointment is strictly temporary and dies the moment Congress adjourns, period. The Constitution provides two separate exit doors: disapproval by the Commission on Appointments, OR the next adjournment of Congress. You do not need an organized Commission for the adjournment door to swing shut; when the session ends—even a short special session—the appointment dies automatically by constitutional clockwork.

---

#### Issue 2: Validity of Congressional Adjournment via Unilateral Senate Adjournment *Sine Die*

**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did the special session of Congress legally adjourn on January 22, 1966, notwithstanding the House’s attempt to suspend its session until January 24, 1966?
**YES.** The Senate’s adjournment *sine die* effectively terminated the special session for the entire bicameral Congress, because one chamber cannot hold a legislative session or transact business independently after the other chamber has adjourned without day.

**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. *Bicameral Nature of Congress:* Under the Constitution, legislative power is vested in a bicameral Congress consisting of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Neither chamber alone constitutes "the Congress."
2. *Legal Impossibility of Independent Session:* When the Senate adjourned *sine die* at midnight of January 22, 1966, the special session of Congress ended in legal contemplation. The House could not unilaterally prolong the special session, because neither house can transact legislative business without the other (referencing the 1954 parliamentary arguments of then-Congressmen Diosdado Macapagal and Cornelio Villareal).
3. *Intervention of Sunday and the Constructive Recess Doctrine:* The contention that the special session merged continuously into the regular session is legally untenable. January 23, 1966, was a Sunday—a day expressly excluded as a constitutional session day. 
4. *Incompatibility of Sessions:* As established in parliamentary law (Hinds’ Precedents), an extraordinary (special) session and a regular session cannot coexist or run seamlessly without interruption. The regular session began by constitutional mandate at 10:00 AM on January 24, which independently closed the special session. There is an inescapable, legal constructive recess dividing them.

**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
> "Although the House allegedly suspended its session at 10:55 p.m. on January 22, 1966 to be resumed on Monday, January 24, 1966, at 10:00 a.m., Congress cannot be considered to be in special session subsequently to January 22 for the reason that the House without the Senate which had adjourned *sine die*, is not 'Congress.' ... An extraordinary session and a regular session can not coexist, and the beginning of the regular session at 12 o'clock was the end of the extraordinary session; not a constructive end of it, but an actual end of it."

**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** One house cannot play Congress by itself. When the Senate packed up and adjourned *sine die* on Saturday night, the special session was legally dead for everyone. Furthermore, special and regular sessions cannot bleed into one another; a Sunday intervened, and parliamentary law mandates a constructive recess between two distinct sessions. The special session had undeniably adjourned.

---

#### Issue 3: Application of the *Aytona* Doctrine on Mass Post-Election Appointments

**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can Petitioner’s *ad interim* appointment be sustained in light of the anti-midnight appointment doctrine?
**NO.** The mass issuance of 1,717 post-election *ad interim* appointments by outgoing President Macapagal represented an even more severe abuse of presidential prerogatives than the 350 appointments invalidated in *Aytona v. Castillo*, providing an independent ground to deny relief.

**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. *Caretaker Administration Principles:* As articulated in *Aytona v. Castillo*, once an outgoing President loses an election, his administration becomes a mere "caretaker" government whose primary constitutional duty is to ensure a smooth, orderly transfer of power to the incoming administration, rather than weaponizing appointments for partisan entrenchment.
2. *Disregard for Fitness and Prerogatives:* President Macapagal issued 1,717 *ad interim* appointments following the November 1965 election, dwarfing the 350 "midnight appointments" struck down in *Aytona*. This frantic scramble resulted in patent absurdities, including appointing a single individual to three distinct judicial salas, appointing a judge to a nonexistent branch in Pangasinan, and appointing a person facing disbarment to a Court of First Instance bench.
3. *Public Policy and Equity:* The writ of *quo warranto* is governed by equitable considerations. The court will not exercise its equitable discretion to validate appointments generated by wholesale abuses of executive prerogative designed to strip the incoming President of constitutional appointing authority.

**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
> "Considering now petitioner's *ad interim* appointment and others extended under similar conditions in the light of the doctrine we laid down in the Aytona case, we may say that they were even more irregular than those involved in said case to the extent that they may be avoided even on this ground alone. Thus, while President Garcia only extended 350 *ad interim* appointments after he had lost the election, President Macapagal made 1,717 *ad interim* appointments most of which were made only after the elections in November, 1965."

**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** If the 350 rushed appointments in *Aytona* were an unconstitutional abuse of power, Macapagal’s 1,717 post-defeat appointments were an absolute mockery of the executive function. Outgoing presidents are mere caretakers. Packing the government with chaotic, unvetted appointments to tie the hands of the incoming administration is contrary to public policy, and the Court will not use its equitable power to protect such appointees.

---

### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight

**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Executive Department | d. Power of Appointment | *Ad Interim* Appointments (Recess Appointments) and Midnight Appointments.

**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
- *Executive Power Exercised:* The President's constitutional prerogative to issue *ad interim* recess appointments to prevent interruption in government functions (1935 Const., Art. VII, Sec. 10[4]).
- *Constitutional Check Invoked:* The legislative confirmation check exercised through the Commission on Appointments and the automatic expiration of tenure upon congressional adjournment.

**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (*Ad Interim* Appointments & Expiration):**
1. *Recess Appointment Power:*
   - *Requirement:* Must be made while Congress is in recess.
   - *Applied:* Guevara was appointed on November 18, 1965, during legislative recess.
2. *Resolutory Condition 1 (Express Disapproval):*
   - *Requirement:* Disapproval by the Commission on Appointments terminates the appointment.
   - *Applied:* Not triggered because the Commission was never organized during the special session.
3. *Resolutory Condition 2 (Legislative Adjournment):*
   - *Requirement:* Automatic expiration upon the "next adjournment of the Congress."
   - *Applied:* Satisfied. The Senate adjourned the special session *sine die* at midnight of January 22, 1966. Congress cannot sit as one house; the special session was adjourned, extinguishing the appointment.
4. *Session Distinctions:*
   - *Requirement:* The Constitution makes no distinction between regular and special sessions.
   - *Applied:* Adjournment of *either* session triggers total expiration.

**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
- *Ad interim appointment* (a permanent appointment subject to a resolutory condition: disapproval or adjournment).
- *Constructive recess* (the required legal separation between a special session and a regular session).
- *Adjournment sine die* (adjournment without assigning a day for a further meeting or hearing; effectively closes the session).
- *Ubi lex non distinguit nec nos distinguere debemus* (where the law does not distinguish, the courts should not distinguish).
- *Caretaker administration* (status of an outgoing presidential administration after an election defeat).

**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
*Guevara v. Inocentes* establishes that under Article VII, Section 10(4) of the 1935 Constitution (now Art. VII, Sec. 16 of the 1987 Constitution), an *ad interim* appointment expires automatically upon the next adjournment of Congress, regardless of whether that session is regular or special, and regardless of whether the Commission on Appointments was ever organized. The Court held that "adjournment" applies to any congressional session under the maxim *ubi lex non distinguit*, and because the Senate adjourned the special session *sine die*, Congress stood adjourned, causing Petitioner Guevara's post-election recess appointment to lapse as a matter of law.

---

### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)

**Separate Opinions Summary:**
- **Concepcion, J., Concurring:** Emphasized that an *ad interim* appointment is subject to both a resolutory condition (disapproval by the Commission) and a resolutory term/period (the next adjournment of Congress). The term/period operates strictly on its own, ensuring the President can re-appoint or select someone else during the next recess to prevent vacancies. A bypass is not an implied disapproval (since bypassed appointees can be re-appointed), but rather an automatic temporal expiration. Furthermore, judicial rewriting of the word "adjournment" to mean "regular session" would amount to unconstitutional judicial legislation.
- **Dizon, J., Concurring:** Fully joined the majority opinion and additionally stressed that Guevara's appointment was invalid under the caretaker doctrine set forth in Justice Sabino Padilla's concurring opinion in *Aytona v. Castillo*.
- **Makalintal, J., Dissenting:** Maintained his earlier dissent from the Court's February 16, 1966 resolution (viewing the adjournment of a brief special session where the Commission was unorganized as insufficient to extinguish recess appointments).

**Verbatim Fallo:**
> "Wherefore, petition is denied. No costs."

**Plain-Language Outcome:** The petition for *quo warranto* was dismissed. Respondent Raoul M. Inocentes was upheld as the lawful Undersecretary of Labor, while Petitioner Onofre P. Guevara was ousted, his *ad interim* appointment having completely lapsed when Congress adjourned its special session.
